Near-field RCS measurements require compensation for spherical wavefront illumination due to shorter antenna-target distances.
The far-field criterion for a 1 m target at 10 GHz requires approximately 70 m separation to ensure planar wavefront illumination.
The proposed technique uses spherical back-projection to correct phase variations caused by spherical waves.
Probe correction compensates for the horn antenna's radiation pattern during image formation.
Radar images are generated by collecting backscattered field data over a wide frequency band (8-12 GHz) and aspect angles.
The target is modeled as a finite number of nondirective point scatterers contributing coherently to the total scattered field.
Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) is used to efficiently compute down-range profiles from frequency data.
The experimental target is a composite aluminum object consisting of a circular cylinder and two cones, about 1 meter long.
Near-field radar images closely resemble far-field images in scattering center location and intensity.
Radar images were generated using 20° aspect regions with 0.2° azimuth steps.
Far-field RCS was calculated from radar images and compared favorably with direct far-field measurements.
The near-field measurements were conducted at a 3.25 m distance, which is in the far-field of the antenna but near-field relative to the target size.
The technique allows RCS estimation over a full 360° azimuth by interpolating images generated at overlapping aspect angles.
Differences in dynamic range between near-field and far-field images are attributed to differences in antenna gain and illumination.
The method can be extended to 3-D radar imaging algorithms for more comprehensive scattering characterization.
The experimental setup included a compact antenna range with a parabolic reflector for far-field measurements and direct horn illumination for near-field measurements.
The radar images show main scattering contributions from structural discontinuities and sharp edges of the target.
The method requires only probe correction for antenna pattern compensation, not full far-field conditions for the target.
The technique was validated in an anechoic chamber at the University of Pretoria, South Africa.
The paper was published in IEEE Transactions on Instrumentation and Measurement, Vol. 45, No. 6, December 1996.
